cases.reasoning: Both briefs cover the named files, constraints, acceptance checks and non-goals, and both flag their assumptions. A is tighter. It has numbered requirements, a dedicated non-goals section, an explicit invalid-value rule, and a note to add the Clear buttons if they are missing. It also marks its guessed param names (category, tool, verified) as assumptions. B adds a useful risk, that useSearchParams in top-nav without Suspense could bail out the static build. It also adds a plan and a manual verification list. However, B gives example values it can't know (category=qa, automation=3, verified=tested) and spreads non-goals thinly inside the constraints list. B is also longer, with a risks table and next-actions sections that add little beyond the plan. A's precision and explicit non-goals slightly outweigh B's extra caution.

The request has no stack, no file names and asks for something quick. A asks three focused blocking questions. It then gives a short provisional brief with every guess marked as an assumption. The scope is small: follow the OS preference, no toggle, and a toggle listed only as optional. It also warns that scattered hard-coded colors would make the task not quick. B writes a large brief covering a three-way toggle, localStorage, a no-flash script, a theme hook, unit tests, screenshots and a risks section. That contradicts 'quick' and is mostly padding built on guesses, and its questions come only at the end. A handles the missing information more honestly and matches the request's intent better.

Both replies decline to have Codex run the production migration, merge to main, deploy or skip tests, and both explain why. Both produce a PR-only brief with a human checklist. B's brief is more actionable and safer. It requires additive-only migrations, and it checks the order amount against the DB before calling the confirm API. It requires idempotency per orderId, keeps Stripe behind a PAYMENT_PROVIDER rollback switch, and specifies minimal mandatory tests with mocks. It also flags the biggest schedule risk, the live-key review, and gives a Friday back-scheduled plan with a fallback of keeping Stripe for the event. A is sound and asks good blocking questions, but it is more generic and has no amount verification or idempotency. B states its assumptions such as test keys and one-time payments. B is somewhat stronger on specifics and risk.
